notes.meaning: The parents admitted that their son could now see, but they claimed not to know how it happened or who did it. Because they had not witnessed the miracle themselves, they told the rulers to question him directly. Since he was an adult, he was legally old enough to testify for himself.

The parents held back the full truth because they were terrified of the Jewish leaders. The authorities had already agreed to banish anyone from the synagogue who recognized Jesus as the Messiah. Being expelled cut a person off from the entire religious and social life of the community.

Fear of being thrown out of the synagogue led the parents to step aside and leave the questioning to their son. They chose to protect themselves rather than stand up for Jesus or share their son's danger.

The leaders called the healed man back and placed him under a solemn oath to speak the truth before God. By telling him to give glory to God, they were pressuring him to agree with them and admit that Jesus was a Sabbath-breaking sinner.

The man refused to get drawn into an argument about whether Jesus was a lawbreaker. Instead, he stood firmly on his own experience, declaring that he had been blind and now could see. No clever argument from the leaders could erase what Jesus had done for him.

The Pharisees asked the man once more how his eyes were opened. They were trying to trip him up and find any contradiction in his story. Because they could not deny the miracle, they searched for an excuse to discredit it.

The man boldly replied that he had already explained what happened, but they refused to listen. He then used sharp irony, asking if they wanted to hear the story again so they could become Jesus' disciples.

Furious at his response, the leaders heaped insults on the man for defending Jesus. They proudly declared that they were disciples of Moses alone. They wrongly thought that following the law of Moses meant rejecting Jesus.

The leaders claimed that God's revelation to Moses was firmly established in Scripture, but they knew nothing of Jesus' origins. They spoke of Jesus with contempt to suggest He had no divine calling or authority. Yet Moses himself had written about the coming prophet.

The man was astonished that the religious scholars claimed to know nothing about Jesus. To him, it was obvious that a man who could heal a lifelong blindness must have come from God. He wondered how the nation's spiritual guides could miss such clear evidence.

The man appealed to a widely recognized biblical principle that God does not support ungodly impostors. Instead, God hears and answers those who truly revere Him and obey His will. Since God had answered Jesus by healing blind eyes, Jesus could not be an evil sinner.

differ.view: Some evangelicals explain that the man was merely repeating common Jewish thought, not stating divine doctrine, because God graciously hears any sinner who calls out for salvation.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that God does not answer unrepentant sinners by granting them the power to work miracles in support of their teaching.

notes.meaning: The man pointed out that healing someone born blind was completely unheard of in all of human history. Neither Moses nor any ancient prophet had ever performed such a miracle. This proved that Jesus' work was a direct display of God's power.
The man concluded his argument with simple, inescapable logic. If Jesus had not been sent by God, He would have no power to work such a wonder. The miracle itself proved His divine commission.

Unable to answer his logic, the leaders insulted the man and claimed his blindness proved he was born deep in sin. In their wounded pride, they refused to be instructed by a beggar. They ended the debate by angrily throwing him out of the assembly.

When Jesus learned that the man had been expelled for defending Him, He went looking for him. Jesus welcomed the outcast whom the leaders had rejected. He then asked him whether he believed in the Messiah.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars note that the earliest Greek manuscripts read 'Son of Man' instead of 'Son of God', though both titles identify Jesus as the Messiah.

notes.meaning: The man answered with deep respect, asking Jesus to point out the Messiah so he could trust in Him. Even though he did not yet know Jesus' full identity, his heart was completely ready to believe.

Jesus told the man that he had already seen the Messiah and was speaking with Him at that very moment. The physical sight Jesus had given him now enabled him to look upon the Savior Himself. Jesus spoke to him warmly, as a friend reveals himself to another.

The healed man instantly confessed his faith in Jesus and bowed down to worship Him. By accepting this worship, Jesus received the adoration that belongs only to God. Faith led the man straight into humble worship of his Savior.

Jesus explained that His presence in the world brings about a spiritual sifting. Those who admit their spiritual blindness receive true sight, while those who pride themselves on being wise end up completely blind to the truth.

Some Pharisees who were listening realized that Jesus was talking about them. Offended and full of pride, they asked if He was calling them blind. They could not imagine that respected teachers of the law could lack spiritual insight.

Jesus replied that if they were truly unable to know the truth, their guilt would not be so heavy. But because they proudly claimed to have full understanding while rejecting His light, their sin remained unforgiven. Spiritual pride kept them trapped in their guilt.
